Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- China's giant pandas are believed to be safe after Monday's earthquake, but concern is growing over how they will get their next meals. The giant pandas' primary food source is bamboo. Authorities confirmed Tuesday that captive animals in two of China's major panda reserves were alive, according to Xinhua, China's official news agency. The Wolong Giant Panda Reserve Center in southwest Sichuan province is home to about 86 giant pandas, who were reported safe Tuesday. Staff and critters at neighboring Chengdu Panda Breeding and Research Center were also reported safe, according to a spokesperson for the Atlanta Zoo, which has two pandas on loan from the wildlife reserve. Concern arose in the international wildlife community over damage to the animals' habitat, as authorities continued assessing the scope of damage in the Sichuan province. The mountainous, densely wooded region is the natural habitat for most of the 1,200 giant pandas living in the wild, making it an obvious location for research bases like Wolong and Chengdu. Giant pandas roam the forest in "open cages" that are meant to provide them with a safe, natural environment that will prepare them for release. With the safety of the pandas confirmed, the animals' caregivers are left to determine how resources like food and medical supplies will reach the bases, which contain breeding facilities and triage centers. Bamboo, the pandas' primary source of food, is a major agricultural product in the region, but whether it can be supplied to the pandas despite infrastructure damage is open to question. "Wolong is hard to access under normal conditions, so the heavy road damage makes it even harder," said Kerry Zobor, spokesperson for the World Wildlife Fund. Zobor said WWF had confirmed the safety of staff based in Beijing, but had not received word on the conditions in Wolong. She said the WWF was also concerned about members who had been touring the country when the earthquake struck. So far, the group has not been located. Scientists in the United States are hopeful that Chinese researchers will adapt to the situation facing them. David Wildt with the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park in Washington says that scientists in Wolong have overcome threats to the giant panda population before. In the late 1990s, the captive giant panda population was in decline, with more animals dying than were born, Wildt said. Thanks to a collaborative effort with American scientists, the Wolong staff was able to reverse the trend. "Our Chinese colleagues are very perceptive when it comes to addressing problems," said Wildt, who has visited Wolong many times as part of the Smithsonian's affiliation with the research base. "Because of their efforts, the population is on the rise today." Wildt said that Chinese scientists have also addressed the issue of alternative food sources before. "Artificial diets in the form of protein biscuits have been created for giant pandas. They're not a complete substitute, but they meet the needs of a basic high-fiber diet," said Wildt, who has worked with two pandas that the Smithsonian has on loan from Wolong. "Right now, we're mostly concerned about the staff. If the staff is fine, then the animals will be fine," Wildt said.

# China's Giant Pandas Confirmed Safe Following Earthquake, But Food Supply Concerns Mount

(CNN) -- China's giant pandas are believed to have survived Monday's earthquake unharmed, though mounting concern now centers on how their next meals will be secured. Bamboo, the primary food source for these iconic animals, remains difficult to access in the earthquake's aftermath.

According to Xinhua, China's official news agency, authorities confirmed Tuesday that captive pandas at two of the country's major reserves had survived the disaster. The Wolong Giant Panda Reserve Center in southwestern Sichuan province, home to approximately 86 giant pandas, was reported safe. Similarly, staff and animals at the neighboring Chengdu Panda Breeding and Research Center were confirmed unharmed, according to a spokesperson for Zoo Atlanta, which has two pandas on loan from the reserve.

Despite this reassuring news, concern has spread throughout the international wildlife community regarding potential damage to the pandas' habitat, as authorities continue assessing the full scope of destruction across Sichuan province. This mountainous, densely forested region serves as the natural habitat for most of the estimated 1,200 giant pandas remaining in the wild, making it a logical site for research facilities such as Wolong and Chengdu. Within these reserves, pandas roam through "open cages" designed to replicate a safe, natural environment that prepares them for eventual release into the wild.

With the animals' immediate safety confirmed, caregivers now face the challenge of determining how essential resources—including food and medical supplies—can reach facilities that house both breeding programs and triage centers. While bamboo is a significant agricultural product in the region, whether it can be delivered to the pandas amid widespread infrastructure damage remains uncertain.

"Wolong is hard to access under normal conditions, so the heavy road damage makes it even harder," explained Kerry Zobor, spokesperson for the World Wildlife Fund (WWF). Zobor noted that while WWF had confirmed the safety of its Beijing-based staff, no word had yet been received regarding conditions at Wolong itself. She added that the organization remains concerned about members who were touring the country when the earthquake struck and whose whereabouts remain unknown.

Scientists in the United States, meanwhile, express confidence that their Chinese counterparts will successfully navigate the crisis. David Wildt of the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park in Washington notes that researchers at Wolong have overcome significant threats to the giant panda population in the past. In the late 1990s, for instance, the captive panda population was in sharp decline, with mortality rates exceeding births. Through a collaborative effort with American scientists, however, Wolong staff successfully reversed this troubling trend.

"Our Chinese colleagues are very perceptive when it comes to addressing problems," said Wildt, who has visited Wolong on numerous occasions through the Smithsonian's affiliation with the research center. "Because of their efforts, the population is on the rise today."

Wildt further noted that Chinese scientists have previously tackled the challenge of alternative food sources. "Artificial diets in the form of protein biscuits have been created for giant pandas. They're not a complete substitute, but they meet the needs of a basic high-fiber diet," explained Wildt, who has worked directly with two pandas on loan to the Smithsonian from Wolong.

"Right now, we're mostly concerned about the staff," Wildt concluded. "If the staff is fine, then the animals will be fine."

# Panda Safety Confirmed After Quake, But Food Supply Remains Uncertain

(CNN) -- Following Monday's devastating earthquake in China, officials believe the nation's beloved giant pandas have survived unharmed—though experts now worry about securing their ongoing food supply. Bamboo, which forms the core of a panda's diet, may prove difficult to obtain in the disaster's aftermath.

Xinhua, China's state news agency, reported Tuesday that panda populations at two of the country's premier conservation centers had come through the disaster safely. The Wolong Giant Panda Reserve Center, located in Sichuan province, houses roughly 86 pandas—all confirmed unharmed as of Tuesday. A representative from Atlanta Zoo, which currently hosts two pandas on loan from the Chinese reserve system, verified that both animals and staff at the nearby Chengdu Panda Breeding and Research Center had also escaped injury.

Despite this reassuring news, wildlife organizations worldwide remain worried about potential destruction to the pandas' natural surroundings, as officials continue evaluating the full extent of damage across Sichuan. This heavily forested, mountainous terrain serves as home to the majority of the world's approximately 1,200 wild giant pandas, which explains why research facilities such as Wolong and Chengdu were established there. At these centers, pandas live within expansive enclosed habitats designed to mimic natural conditions and prepare them for eventual release into the wild.

Now that the animals' immediate safety has been established, caretakers face the challenge of delivering essential supplies—including food and medical resources—to these facilities, which house both breeding programs and emergency care units. While bamboo cultivation represents a significant agricultural activity in the region, earthquake-damaged infrastructure raises serious doubts about whether adequate quantities can reach the reserves.

"Even in the best of circumstances, reaching Wolong presents challenges, and the severe damage to roadways will only compound these difficulties," explained Kerry Zobor, a spokesperson for the World Wildlife Fund.

According to Zobor, WWF staff members stationed in Beijing have been accounted for, though information about conditions specifically within Wolong remains unavailable. Additionally, the organization has expressed concern for members who were traveling through China when the earthquake occurred, as their whereabouts remain unknown.

American researchers remain optimistic that their Chinese counterparts will find ways to navigate the crisis. David Wildt, affiliated with the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park in Washington, points to Wolong's history of successfully managing threats to panda populations. He recalled that during the late 1990s, captive panda numbers were declining as death rates exceeded births. Through joint efforts between American and Chinese researchers, Wolong personnel managed to reverse this troubling pattern.

"Our colleagues in China demonstrate remarkable insight when tackling challenges," noted Wildt, who has made numerous trips to Wolong through the Smithsonian's partnership with the facility. "Their dedication has led to population growth we're seeing today."

Wildt further noted that Chinese scientists have previously developed solutions for alternative nutrition sources. "They've engineered artificial nutrition in the form of protein-enriched biscuits for pandas. While not a perfect replacement for bamboo, these supplements satisfy the basic requirement for a high-fiber diet," said Wildt, whose work includes caring for two Wolong-loaned pandas at the Smithsonian.

He concluded with a note of cautious confidence: "Our primary focus right now is on the wellbeing of the human staff. Once we know they're okay, we can trust that the animals will be properly cared for as well."

# Earthquake Rattles Sichuan's Panda Sanctuaries, Raising Concerns Over Food Supply and Habitat Safety

**CHENGDU, China** — A powerful earthquake that struck Sichuan Province has sent tremors through one of the world's most critical conservation zones, damaging bamboo forests and infrastructure vital to the survival of China's iconic giant pandas, according to wildlife officials and conservation groups monitoring the region.

The quake, which registered significant magnitude and was felt across multiple counties in the mountainous province, triggered landslides in several areas near panda reserves, including regions close to the Wolong National Nature Reserve — one of the most important breeding and rehabilitation centers for the endangered species.

"Our immediate concern is twofold: the physical safety of the pandas and staff, and the integrity of the bamboo forests that sustain them," said a spokesperson for the China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda. "Landslides can wipe out large swaths of bamboo groves in an instant, and pandas depend almost entirely on bamboo for their nutritional needs."

## Bamboo Forests Under Threat

Giant pandas famously consume up to 40 pounds of bamboo daily, and any disruption to this food source can have outsized consequences for a species already vulnerable due to habitat fragmentation. Preliminary reports from reserve rangers indicate that several hillside bamboo corridors — natural pathways pandas use to move between feeding grounds — have been blocked or destroyed by falling debris and shifting terrain.

Environmental researchers warn that even localized damage to bamboo forests can force pandas into unfamiliar territory in search of food, increasing the risk of human-wildlife conflict or exposure to unsafe terrain still settling after the quake.

"Bamboo doesn't regenerate overnight," said Dr. Li Wen, an ecologist who has studied panda habitats for over a decade. "If a significant portion of a reserve's bamboo supply is compromised, it could take years for certain groves to fully recover, and in the meantime, pandas may face nutritional stress."

## Reserve Infrastructure and Staff Respond

Wolong and neighboring reserves, part of the UNESCO-recognized Sichuan Giant Panda Sanctuaries, have activated emergency protocols. Rangers and veterinary staff have been dispatched to assess the condition of both wild and captive panda populations, with drones reportedly being used to survey areas too dangerous for ground teams following the quake.

Some structures at breeding facilities sustained damage, though officials say backup shelters and enclosures remain operational. No panda fatalities have been confirmed at this time, though authorities caution that full assessments are still underway given the rugged and remote nature of much of the affected terrain.

This is not the first time the region's panda population has faced upheaval from seismic activity. The catastrophic 2008 Sichuan earthquake, which claimed tens of thousands of human lives, also damaged panda habitats and forced the temporary relocation of animals from heavily affected centers. Lessons from that disaster have informed updated emergency response protocols now being deployed.

## Long-Term Conservation Concerns

Conservationists say the earthquake underscores the fragility of panda habitats, which remain isolated pockets of forest surrounded by human development, roads, and agriculture — limiting the pandas' ability to migrate naturally in response to environmental disruptions.

The giant panda, once critically endangered, was downgraded to "vulnerable" status in 2016 following decades of conservation investment by the Chinese government and international partners. Advocates worry that natural disasters like this could reverse some of that hard-won progress if bamboo ecosystems and reserve connectivity aren't restored quickly.

International conservation organizations, including the World Wildlife Fund, have expressed solidarity with Chinese wildlife authorities and offered support in assessing ecological damage.

"This earthquake is a stark reminder that conservation success is never permanent," said a WWF representative. "Protecting giant pandas means protecting the entire ecosystem they depend on — and that ecosystem just took a serious hit."

Authorities say a full damage assessment of the reserves, including bamboo coverage loss and habitat viability, is expected within the coming weeks. In the meantime, supplemental feeding programs are reportedly being prepared for pandas in areas where natural bamboo access has been most severely disrupted.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

News of the earthquake's impact reverberated among panda conservation partners worldwide, including the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C., which maintains its own giant panda breeding program and has collaborated with Chinese researchers on panda conservation science for years.

Zoo officials expressed solidarity with their Chinese counterparts and indicated a willingness to provide whatever assistance might be useful, whether through expertise, resources, or coordination with other zoos and conservation bodies that participate in the global panda breeding and research network.

"The panda conservation community is tightly interconnected," a National Zoo representative noted. "What happens at facilities like Wolong affects our shared mission everywhere pandas are studied and protected."

## Looking Ahead

Chinese officials have indicated plans to relocate some pandas from Wolong to other facilities, including reserves and zoos in less affected regions, as repairs to the earthquake-damaged center get underway. The long-term rebuilding effort is expected to take considerable time and resources, with international conservation organizations likely to play a role in fundraising and technical support.

As rescue and recovery operations continued across earthquake-stricken Sichuan Province, the fate of Wolong's panda population remained a focal point for global wildlife advocates, underscoring how natural disasters can threaten not only human communities but also fragile conservation gains decades in the making.
